title: The smell of old books
text: The smell of an old book is chemistry {{1}} as nostalgia. Paper is mostly cellulose, and cellulose {{2}} down slowly in the air, releasing a family of organic compounds — the same molecules, it turns out, as vanilla, almonds and cut grass. A book's particular scent is a {{3}}: the lignin in wood-pulp paper breaks down towards vanilla notes; older rag paper smells of a different {{4}}; and the glue, leather and ink of each edition add their own {{5}}. Libraries have learned to take the chemistry {{6}}. Conservation scientists can date and diagnose a book from its emissions, spotting the acids that mean paper is {{7}} itself apart, and one museum has recorded historic smells so that the sensory past is not {{8}} to the visual alone. The next time a second-hand novel smells of vanilla and smoke, you are not imagining romance — you are smelling the book slowly becoming its own monument.

gaps.explanation: 'chemistry packaged as nostalgia' — presented in an emotional wrapping; parch = dry out.
'cellulose degrades slowly' — decomposes; deflate = lose air or confidence.
'the scent is a blend' — a mixture of notes; bland = flavourless, the sound-alike trap.

gaps.explanation: 'a different palette' — a different range of notes, by the painting metaphor; palate = the roof of the mouth or taste, pallet = a transport platform.
'add their own accents' — their distinguishing notes; ascent = a climb, assent = agreement.
'take the chemistry seriously' — the fixed phrase; sorely = greatly (sorely missed).
'paper is eating itself apart' — consuming itself chemically; ease = make less difficult.
'the sensory past is not restricted to the visual' — confined to; refrain takes 'from'.
